Car Culture · The Long View

The Fastest Argument in the Room

Parliament wanted it stopped. The police could not catch it. And the road testers who actually drove the Lotus Carlton came back saying it was a bit dull. All three were telling the truth.

By Nathaniel Ruiz · 31 minute read

Push the throttle of a Lotus Carlton past halfway and wait about a second. The first turbocharger is already working. Then the second one arrives, and 3,600 pounds of executive saloon stops behaving like transport. Nothing else in the car acknowledges it. The wood-effect trim around the gear lever stays exactly where it is. The rear seats keep their two club armchairs. The boot stays enormous. Only the horizon changes, and it changes at a rate the rest of the interior seems not to have been told about.

That contradiction is the whole car, and in 1990 it made Britain lose its mind.

Within about eighteen months of the Geneva show, a Vauxhall four-door had been condemned by the Association of Chief Police Officers as “an outrageous invitation to speed,” described by the Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents as a high-speed safety hazard, made the target of a Daily Mail campaign to have it banned outright, denounced from the floor of the House of Commons, and used by a gang of ram-raiders who worked out that no police car in Britain could stay with it.

And then the magazines drove it, and came back slightly puzzled.

Everybody spent a year arguing about the number. Almost nobody asked whether the car was any good.

That is the story worth telling, and it is more interesting than the one usually told. The Lotus Carlton is remembered as the car too fast for its own country. What it actually was is a car that became a proxy for an argument about speed — an argument conducted almost entirely by people who had never sat in it. The ones who did sit in it found something more complicated: a machine of genuinely absurd capability that was, at the time, oddly unsatisfying to use.

It took about thirty years for anyone to go back and say the car was brilliant. By then the argument was over, the recession had killed it, and the only people still paying attention were the ones who had wanted one since they were twelve.

The idea that should not have survived a meeting

By the mid-1980s General Motors owned two things that had no business being introduced to one another.

One was Opel, and its British arm Vauxhall, which built the Omega — sold in Britain as the Carlton. It was a genuinely good executive saloon and a completely anonymous one. Its best party trick was aerodynamic: a drag coefficient of 0.28, exceptional for a three-box sedan in 1986, and enough to make modest engines look better than they were. It was European Car of the Year for 1987 largely on that basis. Nobody has ever put a poster of one on a wall.

The other was Lotus, bought in 1986, and fresh from designing the LT5 V8 that turned the Corvette ZR-1 into something Europe had to take seriously.

Mike Kimberley, running Lotus at the time, wanted the Lotus name across the GM Europe range. His first target was not the Carlton at all — it was the larger Senator, and renderings were produced. GM Europe had other ideas, and the project was moved onto the Carlton instead with roughly six weeks left before the 1989 Geneva show.

Six weeks is not a development program. It is a dare.

What Lotus actually changed
  • The engine. The 3.0-liter 24-valve straight six bored out to 3,615cc, on a strengthened, re-webbed block, with Mahle pistons, new rods and a forged steel crankshaft
  • Two Garrett T25 turbochargers, each with its own throttle body and its own water-cooled intercooler
  • New engine management, because the standard system could not be adapted — remapped by AC Rochester, and happiest on high-octane super unleaded
  • The six-speed manual from the Corvette ZR-1, a ZF S6-40, which required cutting and welding the transmission tunnel to fit
  • A limited-slip differential from the V8 Holden Commodore in Australia
  • AP brakes — 12.9-inch ventilated front discs on four-piston calipers, 11.8 inch at the rear
  • Suspension reworked throughout: an extra link added to each semi-trailing arm, self-leveling rear dampers, front struts and steering geometry redrawn
  • Bodywork — arch extensions, front and rear bumpers and sills in fiberglass, and a rear wing. On the Geneva show car the wing extended automatically above 100 mph. The production car got a fixed one, which worked just as well and cost rather less

Those front discs deserve a moment. At 12.9 inches they are larger in diameter than the entire road wheel of any Mini built after 1984, when the classic went from ten-inch wheels to twelve. Against a 1960s Mini the brake disc wins by three inches.

Built twice, on purpose

The manufacturing arrangement is the detail that tells you how serious this was, and how absurd.

Opel built the donor cars — ordinary Omega and Carlton 3000 GSi saloons — on a dedicated line at Rüsselsheim in Germany. When there were enough to fill a transporter they were shipped across the North Sea to Hethel, in Norfolk, where Lotus took them completely apart. The engines and gearboxes came straight back out and were returned to Germany to be used again on the line, shuttling back and forth to build the next batch. Brakes and hubs were simply scrapped rather than reused on a customer car. The bodies arrived painted and were then cut into anyway, to widen the transmission tunnel and take the arch extensions.

Assembly happened in Factory 3 at Hethel — the building Lotus had used as its engineering center for the DeLorean, which is the kind of coincidence you could not put in a novel. Each car took somewhere between 130 and 150 hours depending on whose account you believe; Kimberley’s own figure is 130.

Vauxhall’s press material of the day said each engine was hand-assembled by one of just five men, and that every car received a thousand new components. Both lines have been repeated for thirty-five years and I cannot find a source for either that is not ultimately that same press pack. They may well be true. Treat them as marketing until somebody produces the paperwork.

A good story that does not survive a tape measure

You will read, in more than one otherwise careful account, that Lotus started with the block from the Omega diesel, on the grounds that it was cast thicker and stronger. It is a lovely detail and the engineering logic behind it is sound — Opel’s cam-in-head diesels did get stiffened blocks and longer strokes, and Lotus did go looking for a longer stroke.

It does not fit. The Lotus six needs a 95mm bore. The largest of the CIH diesels managed 92mm. There is no version of that block with the bore centers to get there. What Lotus actually used was the 3.0-liter petrol block with additional webbing. The diesel story probably started because every CIH diesel used an 85mm stroke — which is exactly the stroke Lotus adopted.

Vauxhall Lotus Carlton / Opel Lotus Omega, 1990–92

Torque419 lb-ft @ 4,200 rpm · compression 8.2:1

Never sold in the United States. It became legally importable in 2011 under the NHTSA’s Show or Display exemption, a decade before the 25-year rule caught up with it.

What the numbers meant in 1990

Mercedes and BMW had agreed among themselves to limit their fast saloons to 155 mph. Vauxhall had not been invited to that conversation, and would not have accepted.

Look at where the Vauxhall lands, and then look at how little separates the top four. Three tenths of a second covers a 911 Turbo, a Ferrari flagship and a Vauxhall with a parcel shelf. That is not a ranking; that is the same afternoon on slightly different tires. The Carlton did not beat the supercars and it did not lose to them either. It stood in the group photograph, which nothing with four doors and a full-size boot had ever done before.

The BMW M5 is the one it genuinely walked away from — a second and a half back, and that was the car it was actually built to embarrass.

Andrew Frankel, who tested the thing for Autocar when it was new, put the Ferrari comparison more bluntly than any chart can. Running the numbers on both cars, the magazine found the Carlton was quicker to 60 mph, quicker from 30 to 70, and identical over a standing quarter mile. “The Ferrari flagship of the time, the Testarossa, produced just 17 more horsepower,” he wrote, “and when the subject turned to torque, Maranello’s flagship was utterly trounced.”

That is the comparison that should have ended the argument before it started. Ferrari money — £106,998, about $191,000 at the exchange rate of the day, or a shade under half a million in 2026 dollars — bought you a Testarossa. Forty-five percent of it bought you a car that arrived at 60 mph at the same moment and could take three friends and their luggage while it did.

Evo once did the arithmetic on how far ahead of its own class the Carlton really was, taking its margin over the 1990 M5 and scaling it forward to the M5 of the magazine’s day: you would need, the magazine reckoned, a saloon with 662 bhp and 791 lb-ft to reproduce the gap. Its phrase for that was “a family-sized four-door with the performance of a McLaren F1.”

The gearing joke

Here is a detail that sounds like a myth and turns out to be arithmetic.

The Carlton has six speeds because the Corvette ZR-1 had six speeds, and sixth is enormously tall — a cruising overdrive rather than a gear you would ever use in anger. It is so tall that the car is faster in fifth.

This is not a quirk somebody noticed. It falls straight out of the ratios. In sixth the car covers about 44 mph for every thousand rpm, so holding the claimed 176 mph asks the engine for barely 4,000 — more than a thousand revolutions below where it makes its power. In fifth the same speed needs just over 6,000 rpm, which is exactly where you want to be.

Which means the fastest four-door in the world had a top gear you could not use to reach its top speed. The engineers were not building for the traffic-light drag race, and they were not really building for the record either. They were building for a very long, very empty road.

The scandal

No car this fast, wearing four doors and a Vauxhall badge, was ever going to arrive quietly. What nobody at GM seems to have anticipated is how long the outrage would have to build.

The Lotus Omega prototype appeared at Geneva in March 1989. Customer cars did not arrive until late 1990. That left something over a year in which the only thing anyone knew about the car was its top speed — which is the worst possible way to introduce a machine whose actual character is subtle.

The Association of Chief Police Officers called it an outrageous invitation to speed. The Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents made it the centerpiece of a campaign against manufacturers advertising performance at all. The Daily Mail ran a campaign to have it banned. And on Friday, November 16, 1990, it reached the House of Commons.

Hansard, Road Safety debate, November 16, 1990

“Will the hon. Gentleman join me in condemning especially the heavy publicity that has been given recently to a Vauxhall Carlton which is capable, apparently, of achieving 170 mph? It should not be available for public purchase, even at the outrageous price of, I think, £45,000.”

Alex Carlile MP, Montgomery

“These are cars which require the skill of Nigel Mansell to operate them safely. In an earlier age, we would have expected only Stirling Moss or Fangio, or others of that nature, to operate them… It is absurd that such cars should be made available on a large scale because there is no place where they can be driven at the speeds of which they are capable.”

Sir Anthony Grant MP, Cambridgeshire South-West

“I understand that General Motors and Vauxhall are not selling the 470 high-speed Carltons that will be available… without the purchasers and future users having gone through a test.”

Roger King MP, Birmingham Northfield — defending it

The motoring press was not united behind the car either. Autocar’s own editor, Bob Murray, wrote that “nobody buying this car could possibly argue he either needs or will be able to use a top whack which is claimed to be around 180 mph,” and proposed that Vauxhall follow the Germans and limit it to 155. The magazine that would shortly go out and try to measure the thing was on record saying it should not have been allowed to go that fast.

You will often read that the Lotus Carlton is the only production car ever debated in Parliament. It is a great line and it is not true on any of its three parts. There was no debate on the car — it came up in interventions during a general road safety debate. Hansard does not call it a Lotus; the phrase used is “a Vauxhall Carlton.” And cars get named in Parliament all the time, on safety, emissions, tax and industry.

The true version needs no help. A Member of Parliament stood up and said a car on sale in Britain should not be available for anyone to buy, and another compared operating it to the job of a Formula One World Champion. That happened, it is in the record, and Vauxhall had to sit and read it.

What Vauxhall did next

Under that pressure, the company blinked in one direction and refused to blink in the other.

It blinked on advertising: Vauxhall announced it would stop quoting top speeds in any of its car advertising, while continuing to quote 0–60 times, which is the kind of distinction that only makes sense to a public relations department under fire. It also offered Carlton buyers high-speed driving tuition, which was either responsible or an admission, depending on which newspaper you read.

What it would not do was fit a limiter.

This part is usually told as a boardroom vote — GM executives sitting around a table and unanimously deciding to hold the line. I can find no evidence of a vote. What is documented is more human and more interesting: Vauxhall and Opel disagreed. Opel wanted a 155 mph governor, in line with the Germans. Vauxhall did not. Vauxhall won.

The car left the factory unrestricted not because a boardroom was brave, but because one national sales company argued harder than the other.

Then the ram-raiders got hold of one. A gang used a Lotus Carlton registered 40 RA through a six-week run of raids, on the entirely correct reasoning that nothing in the police fleet could follow it. The car was eventually pulled out of a canal near Knowle with its plates still fitted, and the Birmingham Post ran the headline “Taunted by the world’s fastest ram-raiders” in January 1994.

The detail that gets repeated — that police Senators were limited to 150 mph — is wrong, and the truth is worse. Autocar’s road test of the Senator 3.0i 24v recorded a top speed of 139 mph and 0–60 in 9.1 seconds. There was no limiter. That was simply the car. Britain’s pursuit vehicle was 37 mph slower than the thing it was chasing, and four seconds behind it to 60.

And then somebody drove it

Here is the turn in the story, and it is the part that almost never gets told.

While Parliament was worrying about 176 mph and the tabloids were demanding a ban, the road testers went out in the thing — and what came back was admiration rather than delight.

What the period press actually said

“The problem is the driver can only get so involved — with its dull-sounding engine, ponderous gearchange, feel-less steering and heavily damped responses, it is a little short on aural and tactile stimulation.”

Autocar & Motor, quoted in Lotus: The Creative Edge — the same review calls it “as gentle and benign as a pussycat”

“The Lotus Carlton reached this speed with such finesse and lack of fireworks that one felt ‘so what’, it was that impressive.”

Motor Sport, December 1990 — which also noted a rattling gear lever knob

Read those twice, because they are doing something unusual. Neither is saying the car is slow, or bad, or overrated. They are saying it is so competent that using it produces no sensation. The engine is muted. The shift is heavy and long. The steering tells you little. The damping absorbs the drama before it reaches you. It goes monstrously fast and hands back almost nothing while it does it.

“So what,” wrote Motor Sport, “it was that impressive.” That is a sentence with a genuine ache in it.

So the argument raging outside the car and the experience inside it had almost nothing to do with each other. Britain was frightened of a number. The people qualified to judge the machine found the number was the least involving thing about it.

And nobody ever proved the number anyway.

The record nobody actually set

Vauxhall claimed 176 mph, from a GM test. In 1990 Autocar tried to verify it and reached 163.6 mph before running out of road, reporting that the car was still pulling and reckoning at least another ten in it. That is the closest a magazine got at the time.

The best independently measured figure came almost thirty years later, when Hagerty took one to Bruntingthorpe in 2019 and recorded about 170 mph on GPS — in fifth, and with the aerodynamics of a large saloon body doing exactly what large saloon bodies do above 150.

Three claims to retire

That Autocar sent Richard Noble to Bruntingthorpe. Noble is real and he did run a Carlton — but it was at Elvington, it was a Vauxhall in-house exercise run by the company’s Malcolm Tearle, and it happened years later, alongside a Monaro. Tearle’s recollection of 186 mph is a reading of where the speedometer needle was pointing, not a measurement.

That it did 177, or 179, or over 180. 177 is 284 km/h converted and rounded. 179 traces to a single enthusiast site. “Over 180” is a test driver’s anecdote. The LHD Omega was certified to 182 mph, which is a paperwork exercise, not a run.

That the number was ever settled. It was not. The honest sentence is that Vauxhall claimed 176 mph, nobody disproved it, and nobody proved it either.

Which is a strangely fitting end to the whole affair. The country spent a year and a parliamentary session arguing about a figure that no one has ever actually recorded.

The gym, and the finishing school

All of the above is about a number. Almost none of it is about the car, and the car is the thing 950 people actually had to reverse into parking spaces.

Start with what it was before Hethel got it. A Carlton 3000 GSi was a rep’s reward and a sales director’s company motor — a large, sensible, slightly dull Luton saloon that spent its life on the M6 with a suit hanging behind the driver’s seat. Everything Lotus did left that car intact underneath. The doors still shut with the same slightly hollow thump. The rear bench still swallows three adults. The boot is still 18.4 cubic feet, and folding the seats still gets you to nearly 31.

It is a blue-collar car that has been to the gym and then, separately, to finishing school. Neither trip removed the accent.

Around town, which is where most of them lived

The first thing every single person who has driven one mentions is the clutch. Not the power, not the noise. The clutch.

CAR’s modern verdict is that it is “by far the heaviest clutch I have ever experienced in a car, requiring thighs of steel when you’re stuck in traffic.” Evo’s Richard Meaden wrote it out as “the clutch pedal is r-e-a-l-l-y heavy.” Retro Motor, driving Vauxhall’s own preserved press car in 2024, found that the only thing giving the game away at low speed “is the clutch, which requires a committed shove.” A Lotus Carlton in a supermarket car park is a leg workout with air conditioning.

The gearchange is the other one. The ZF six-speed came out of the Corvette ZR-1 and it drives like it. Autosport called it agricultural in November 1990 and thirty-five years of testers have essentially agreed: “industrial shift quality” (Evo), “a huge throw” (Retro Motor), “ponderous” (Autocar & Motor, at the time). The only dissenting voice is the one that logged the most miles — Autocar’s 20,000-mile long-term car, whose report concluded that the steering, clutch, gearshift and brakes were all “firm and precise to use, demanding deliberate but not excessively heavy use.” Which is a very British way of saying you get used to it.

What you do not get is drama. There is remarkably little turbo lag for a 1990 twin-turbo — 0.7 bar of boost is in by 2,500 rpm and 347 lb-ft is already there at 2,000, so the car pulls cleanly from almost anywhere without asking you to plan ahead. First gear runs to 55 mph. In practice that means most town driving happens in first and second with the engine barely awake, at which point the Lotus Carlton is exactly as demanding as the Carlton it used to be, plus the clutch.

The steering argument, which is really an argument about 1990

Here is a genuine and unresolved split in the record. In January 1991, What Car? praised Lotus specifically for having “worked wonders by ridding the Carlton of the slightly vague patch in steering feedback around the straight ahead position,” adding that “response is immediate, whereas the standard car takes rather more effort.”

Every modern tester describes exactly that vague patch. CAR: “a ginormous dead spot on the straight-and-narrow, almost to old Hollywood movie levels.” Retro Motor: “a little disconnected at town speeds.” Evo: “accurate and well-weighted — it’s also a bit numb.”

Either thirty-five years of wear has put the slack back into surviving cars, or the goalposts moved and nobody sent Lotus a memo. Probably both. It is worth knowing before you read another word of praise or criticism about how this car steers.

Then you find a good road

This is a Lotus, so the suspension is the part you are entitled to have expectations about. It largely meets them, in a way that has aged strangely well.

The period verdict was unambiguous. What Car?, January 1991: “Thanks to the odd Lotus tweak to the front and rear suspension set-ups, this Carlton has quite outstanding agility. There’s virtually no inertia or yaw when flicking from one direction to another through a sequence of bends which, for its size, is remarkable.” Autocar’s long-termer, two and a half years later, noted “the suspension was compliant despite the huge tyres and the absence of body roll in hard corners.”

Drive one now and the description flips, without the car having changed at all. Evo: “The suspension set-up is very different to a modern car — you get a supple, settled feel with plenty of roll through the corners.” What read as flat body control in 1991 reads as lean in 2026, because everything built since has been tied down harder and given up ride quality to do it.

The balance is the good bit, and it is consistent across every account. There is gentle understeer to lean on into a corner, and then, as Evo puts it, “in tighter corners it’s happy to smoke its rear tyres with a big, progressive and easily held slide.” Richard Hammond, who took one round a test track for Top Gear, called it “the most slidey thing in which I have ever slithered” — while noting that the rear end “glides about apparently at whim, but always remaining respectfully behind the front end.” That last clause is the entire chassis in eleven words. The car will absolutely go sideways. It will not surprise you when it does.

Power delivery, per Hammond, arrives “in the same way Vinnie Jones might slam your head in a car door,” which is the least Norfolk sentence ever written about a Lotus and also completely accurate.

And the brakes are extraordinary — still, now, thirty-six years on. The period road test called them “simply the best brakes we’ve yet encountered on a road car.” That is not a period exaggeration, and there is a number to prove it, which we will get to in a moment.

Andrew Noakes, who has been writing about this car since it was new, summarized the surprise better than anybody: “I’d expected it to be a thuggish, intimidating beast. That it turns out to be nothing of the sort is a huge, and welcome, surprise.”

And then a very long straight one

This is what it was actually built for, and the gearing gives it away before the chassis does. At 44 mph per thousand rpm in sixth, a Lotus Carlton doing 70 on a motorway is turning under 1,600 rpm. It is not working. It is idling toward Germany.

Everyone who has taken one past three figures reports the same thing, which is nothing. PistonHeads: “The car feels totally planted on the motorway and it was undoubtedly developed with high-speed cruising in mind.” Hagerty UK, running one at Bruntingthorpe until the phone GPS flickered to 170 in fifth: “the Carlton’s stability was peerless.” Evo, sitting at 165 on a German autobahn: it “sits there, not quite rock-steady, but stable enough to keep the throttle pinned.”

Andrew Frankel’s version is the one that makes your palms damp. Testing the car new at Millbrook, he arrived at the end of the straight at 160 mph and had to put a large saloon onto steep banking at a speed nobody had tried before. His entire account of what happened next is two words: it stuck.

The overtake is the party trick nobody warned people about in 1990. PistonHeads again: “40 to 70 mph goes in the blink of an eye, the surge so severe I don’t have time to look.” In third gear the car covers 50 to 70 mph in 2.8 seconds. That is the single most useful number in this entire article, and it is the one Parliament should have been worried about, because it is not a racetrack figure. It is a B-road figure. It is what happens when a Lotus Carlton decides to get past a caravan.

Living with one, according to the people who did
  • Boot: 18.4 cubic feet — 30.7 with the rear seats folded. Unchanged from the ordinary Carlton
  • Interior: Connolly leather throughout, including the wheel, gear knob and door trims. Full air conditioning, extending to a cooled glovebox
  • Seats: reclining sports buckets with two-way lumbar and height adjustment on both sides — unusual in 1990
  • Service intervals identical to a Vauxhall Nova. First service on Autocar’s long-termer: £136.54, about $205 at the time. The 9,000-mile oil service: £115.02
  • Rear tires: 265/40 ZR17, at just over £190 fitted — roughly $285 then, and you will not be getting 20,000 miles out of them
  • Reliability over 20,000 miles: “First class; no breakdowns or threats of same.” The only damage the car sustained was from an attempted theft
  • What actually goes wrong: timing chains, catastrophically, if maintenance slips. Viscous fans, on cars left standing. Clutches, expensively. And corrosion hiding behind the fiberglass arch extensions where nobody looks

Sources: Autocar’s 20,000-mile long-term report, April 21, 1993; Vauxhall’s own specification material; Octane’s 2024 buying guide. Note that the Recaro seats often credited to this car are not documented anywhere — the seats are Vauxhall’s own sports items, in Connolly hide.

Which is the part that makes the whole thing cohere. It is a 377 bhp twin-turbo built by Lotus in the DeLorean building, and it was serviced on a Nova schedule, went 20,000 miles without a fault, and had somewhere to put a suit carrier. The gym did not take away the day job.

The comparison test it never got

Here is a gap in the record that says more about 1990 than any road test does.

The Lotus Carlton never appeared in a period group test against the cars it was built to beat. There is no Autocar four-way against the M5, the 500E and the Sierra Cosworth. There is no CAR shootout with an Alpina B10. The obvious feature — the fastest saloon on earth versus everything else with four doors — simply never ran while the car was on sale.

There are reasons. Only 950 were built and press cars were scarce. Britain’s allocation collapsed with the economy. And by the time customer cars arrived in late 1990, the Carlton had stopped being a car in editorial terms and become a controversy; the commissioning question was no longer is it better than an M5, it was should this be legal. The magazines wrote the story the country was having.

What it did get, in August 1992, was one genuine contest — and it is a much better one.

Autocar & Motor took a group of cars to Santa Pod for a 0–100–0 mph challenge: standing start to 100 mph, then back to a dead stop. Lotus development engineer Rudy Thomann drove the Carlton. Nick Mason’s Ferrari F40 won at 15.9 seconds. The Vauxhall came second at 17.2. A Ford RS200 — a Group B rally car with a numberplate — came third at 18.9.

The magazine’s own account of what that felt like is worth quoting, because it is the period press finally finding the language for this car:

Autocar & Motor, Santa Pod, August 5, 1992

“The phenomenal acceleration of a Lotus Carlton is a strange thing to experience because of the apparent lack of drama.”

The same sentence, essentially, that Motor Sport wrote in 1990 — but now framed as a compliment

“For the next 5.8 secs I’m the dummy in the Volvo crash commercial, thrown forward into the seatbelt.”

On the braking — 100–0 mph in 5.15 seconds at best, “nearly a second better than any of the other standard production cars”

Read that second one again. In the only head-to-head the Lotus Carlton ever entered, the thing it did better than anything else present was stopping. A four-door saloon with a parcel shelf, at Santa Pod, out-braking the field.

What happened when the comparison finally came

The test that never ran in period has been run several times since, and the Carlton’s record is honest rather than flattering.

Evo put it on a German autobahn against an F10-generation M5 in 2013 and declined to declare a winner, which was the correct call — the modern car is faster, safer and more capable in every measurable way, and Richard Meaden still wrote that “there’s something magical about the dark green Lotus Carlton… for one glorious afternoon it owned the Autobahn.” His complaint about the BMW is the one that matters: “to feel it strain at its electronic restrictor like a dog on a leash is incredibly frustrating.” The Carlton had no leash. That is the whole point of it, and in 2013 it was the only car in the photograph that could still say so.

A three-way retrospective against the Alpina B10 Bi-Turbo and the Mercedes 500E — the two cars that were genuinely its contemporaries — went the other way. The Alpina won. The Mercedes was called “a seamless surge” but “remote and disinterested.” The Carlton was credited with “a wonderfully, defiantly GM feel” and then filed under cars where the driver has to work for the performance rather than being handed it. Which is, depending on your temperament, either the criticism or the reason.

Thirty-five years of testing produces a fairly stable verdict, and it is not the one the tabloids wrote. The Lotus Carlton is not the most exciting super-saloon ever built and it is not the most polished. It is the one with the widest gap between what it looks like and what it does, and it is the one nobody was allowed to limit.

Killed by the accountants, not the campaigners

For all the noise, nothing was ever banned. No legislation was passed. The car that Parliament wanted off the road was seen off by something far more ordinary.

It cost £48,000 in 1990 — about $85,600 at the exchange rate of the day, and something like $219,000 in 2026 money. That was more than twice a fully-loaded Vauxhall Senator and about £4,500 more than a BMW M5. By 1992 it was five pounds short of £50,000, and the market for expensive cars had fallen out of the bottom of the British economy. The plan had been 1,100 cars, with 440 of them right-hand drive for Britain. Britain’s allocation was cut to 285 — plus one unofficial extra, built at Hethel from a damaged shell that workers at Rüsselsheim had repaired rather than scrapped — and only around 250 found buyers.

Production stopped late in 1992, 150 cars short, at 950: 320 Vauxhall Carltons and 630 Opel Omegas. Every single one Imperial Green. No factory exception has ever been documented.

It was not a ban. It was an empty order book.

Eight years, not ten

The line you will see everywhere is that it took the better part of a decade for another saloon to out-power the Carlton. It took eight years, and it was closer than that makes it sound.

In 1994 Mercedes offered the E60 AMG, an option code on the 500E, with 375 bhp and 428 lb-ft. It out-torqued the Lotus Carlton comfortably and came within two horsepower of it — and Mercedes built about forty-five of them, which is why nobody remembers. The first four-door built in real numbers to clearly beat 377 bhp was the E39 M5 in 1998.

Eight years, in a decade when everything else in the car industry was moving faster than it ever had. That is the actual measure of what Lotus did in Norfolk with six weeks’ notice.

Thirty years later, everyone changed their mind

The reappraisal, when it came, was total.

The modern verdict

“Third to fourth is a sweet spot… the turbos spool and you add speed at a rate more in keeping with today’s hyper-hatches than a 30-year-old saloon with plastic interior wood trim. Experience this hit just once and you’re hooked.”

Evo

“It’s like a nightclub bouncer who’s worked on the circuit for some time. He’s getting on a bit but he’s still sharply dressed, still works out extensively and still more than willing to knock your block off if you wind him up.”

CAR

“The back-end loves to get loose, but with the long wheelbase and lovely steering feel you have the confidence to rein it all in — the joy comes from taming the Carlton.”

CarThrottle, December 2018

“The car that rewrote, publicised and defined the supersaloon class.”

Top Gear, 2017 — leaving it off a greatest-super-saloons list only because it predates the magazine

Notice what changed, because it is not the car. Nobody went back and fixed the gearchange or gave the engine a better voice. What changed is everything the Carlton is now measured against.

In 1990 it was judged beside cars that also had hydraulic steering, also had a manual gearbox, and also told you what the front axle was doing. On that field its damping and its muted six read as remoteness. Put the same car next to something built in 2026 — electrically assisted, turbocharged through a filter, tuned in software — and “heavily damped” becomes composure, and “feel-less steering” becomes, in CarThrottle’s words, steering feel the new boys would kill for.

The car did not improve. The alternative got worse.

What one costs now

Tidy cars now start somewhere around £45,000, which is about $60,000. Good ones sit in the £60,000 to £85,000 band — call it $80,000 to $114,000. And twice now the very best have gone past six figures in pounds: £111,524 at Historics in December 2023 for a car with under 18,000 miles, and £109,125 at Iconic in May 2026. Both of those are around $146,000 to $149,000.

But look at the spread in that chart before you get excited. A car made £109,125 in May of this year, and another made £42,750 — about $57,000 — eight weeks earlier. One failed to sell at all in 2025. Nine hundred and fifty cars is not a market, it is a rumor — condition and mileage are doing nearly all the work, and a single bad example can drag a whole year’s data sideways.

For Americans there is a footnote worth knowing: it was never sold here, and it never had to be. It became legally importable in 2011 under the Show or Display exemption, a decade before the 25-year rule would have got there anyway. One sold on Bring a Trailer in April of this year for $50,500. They are arriving.

The verdict

The Lotus Carlton was not the most exciting car of 1990. Several period testers said so at the time and they were not wrong, and the honest version of this story has to include that.

What it was is something rarer: a car that was allowed to be finished. Six weeks from a decision to a show stand, a bored-out block, somebody else’s gearbox, an Australian differential, a rear wing, and no limiter — not because a boardroom was brave, but because one sales company argued harder than the other and nobody stopped them in time.

Then it sat there for two years being shouted at by police chiefs, safety campaigners, tabloid editors and Members of Parliament, none of whom had driven it, while the people who had driven it quietly reported that it was tremendously fast and slightly cold. And then a recession killed it, and it went away 150 cars short of its own target.

Every part of that is unrepeatable. Not the engineering — a modern manufacturer could build a 377 bhp four-door before lunch, and several of them do. What is unrepeatable is the whole shape of the thing: the willingness to ship a car that a government minister had objected to on the record, the absence of anyone senior enough to say no, and a company small enough that six weeks and a good argument could still change the plan.

They would run the clinics now. They would model the risk, poll the sentiment, and fit the limiter. And they would be right to.

The Carlton is the last four-door that got out of the building before somebody sensible saw it.

Nine hundred and fifty cars. All Imperial Green. Never officially proved to do what everyone was frightened of.

And thirty-six years on, the argument is finally over, and the car turned out to be the good bit.

Sources and further reading Parliamentary record: Hansard, House of Commons Road Safety debate, November 16, 1990 — the Carlile, Grant and King quotations are taken directly from it. Engineering, production and period context: Lotus: The Creative Edge (the Autocar & Motor quotation, the Rüsselsheim shuttle arrangement, the DeLorean building and the Group C brake lineage are attributed to that book); Mike Kimberley’s recollections via Hagerty UK; Autocar’s Luton-to-Hethel feature, which is the source for the Elvington run and the Vauxhall–Opel disagreement over the governor. Period road tests: Motor Sport, December 1990; CAR’s 1990 M5-versus-Testarossa twin test; Autocar’s Senator 3.0i 24v road test. Modern reappraisals: Evo; CAR; CarThrottle, December 2018; Top Gear, 2017; Hagerty UK’s 2019 Bruntingthorpe run. Ram-raid history: Classic & Sports Car on the 40 RA car, and the Birmingham Post, January 7, 1994. Driving and ownership material: What Car?, January 1991; Autosport, November 8, 1990; Autocar & Motor’s 0–100–0 Challenge, August 5, 1992; Autocar’s 20,000-mile long-term report, April 21, 1993; Evo’s 2013 autobahn twin test with the F10 M5; Andrew Frankel writing for Goodwood on his period Millbrook run; Richard Hammond for Top Gear; PistonHeads; Retro Motor; Octane’s buying guide; Andrew Noakes. Values: classic.com transaction data, Historics, Iconic Auctioneers, Artcurial and Bring a Trailer. Currency converted at the 1990 annual average of $1.78 to the pound and inflated on US CPI-U. Gearing figures calculated from the published ratios.

Claims deliberately left out That every engine was built by one of five men, and that each car received a thousand new components — both trace to Vauxhall’s 1990 press material and no further. That the block came from the Omega diesel — the bore dimensions rule it out. That GM executives voted unanimously against a limiter — no record of a vote exists. That police Senators were limited to 150 mph — the Senator could not reach 150. That it is the only production car ever debated in Parliament — it was mentioned, not debated, and the superlative is false. That the Carlton had Recaro seats — no source documents it; the hide is Connolly and the seats are Vauxhall’s own. That it did 177 mph — there is no primary source for that figure; 176 is the only claim with a test behind it.
